lesson.title: Naming an Endpoint: The Socket Address
lesson.summary: A socket address pairs an IP address with a port number to identify not just a machine on the network, but a specific application running on it, and nearly every sockets API call depends on one.
lesson.body:
A socket address is the combination of an IP address and a port number, and together the two identify a specific communication endpoint, not merely a machine on the network, but a particular application, or a particular running instance of one, on that machine.

It helps to see why neither piece alone is enough. An IP address identifies a host, but a single host can be running many different network applications at the same time, perhaps a web server and a mail server on the very same machine. The port number is what distinguishes between them, a number a process claims for its own exclusive use, so that traffic arriving for that port gets delivered to the right process rather than to whichever program happens to be listening first. The pair, IP address together with port, is a complete description of reach this particular program on this particular machine, which is exactly what a socket address is for.

This concept turns out to be central to the Berkeley sockets API, because nearly every socket operation needs a socket address for something: to say where a socket should receive traffic, as with bind(); to say where a socket should send traffic, as with connect() for TCP or on every call to sendto() for UDP; or to report where an incoming connection came from, as accept() does when it hands back a newly connected socket. That is exactly why socket address deserves its own chapter before diving into bind, listen, accept, and connect individually, each of those operations leans on this same idea.

As a concrete example, a web server handling HTTPS traffic might have the socket address 203.0.113.10:443, combining its IP address 203.0.113.10 with port 443. A browser connecting to that server has a socket address of its own too, built from its local IP address and an ephemeral port the operating system picked automatically, something like 198.51.100.7:52344. The pair of these two socket addresses, source and destination together, along with the protocol in use, uniquely identifies one particular TCP connection, which is exactly how an operating system can juggle many simultaneous connections arriving at the very same server port without ever confusing one client's data for another's.
